source.title: Better and Worse with Scale: How Contextual Entrainment Diverges with Model Size
source.authors: Dikshant Kukreja; Kshitij Sah; Gautam Gupta; Avinash Anand; R. Shah; Zheng-Kui Wang; Aik Beng Ng; Erik Cambria

record.file_problem: The paper text is present through its appendices. Some figures are garbled in the extracted text, but the relevant tables and descriptions are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures contextual entrainment across model sizes and mentions induction-head circuits as a possible interpretation, but it does not measure induction heads, the induction pattern, training-time formation, or in-context-learning loss by token position.
record.gate_note: The paper measures context-induced logit shifts for distractor and gold tokens, not induction-head behavior. It cites induction heads as a possible account of mechanical copying and says mechanistic decomposition is future work. The rows record the primary distractor-entrainment measure and its scaling fits; the paper's relative-advantage and gold-token results are left out under the 60-row cap.
record.test_reason: The study measures contextual entrainment: logit shifts of distractor tokens when context is prepended, fitted as power laws across Cerebras-GPT and Pythia sizes. It never identifies or ablates induction heads or previous-token heads. It has no training-time trajectory and no in-context-learning loss by token index. Induction heads appear only as a cited interpretation (via Niu et al.) of mechanical copying and as future work in the limitations. Copy-like behaviour toward arbitrary context tokens is a related but different construct, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. The authors find that entrainment follows power laws with opposite-signed exponents: negative for semantic contexts, positive for non-semantic ones. The pattern replicates across Cerebras-GPT and Pythia. They interpret this as semantic filtering and mechanical copying scaling in opposition. They state that no mechanistic decomposition into heads or circuits was done.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses contextual logit-shift measurements and power-law fits across model sizes, following the contextual-entrainment setup of Niu et al. It does not identify or intervene on induction heads, or analyze training-time formation. It reports relative-advantage and gold-token measures in addition to distractor shifts.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured scaling direction differs by context type (Related, Irrelevant, Random, Counterfactual); the study reports the sign split in both Cerebras-GPT and Pythia.

fits_no_version.finding: Distractor logit boosts scale with model size in opposite directions by context type. Semantic contexts give negative exponents (Counterfactual and Related). Non-semantic contexts give positive exponents (Random and Irrelevant). This holds in both Cerebras-GPT and Pythia.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Contextual entrainment has context-dependent scaling: semantic distractor boosts fall with model size, while non-semantic (mechanical copying) boosts rise.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The paper explicitly does not analyze individual heads, layers, or circuits. It studies decoder-only Transformers from two model families and notes that other architectures and attention variants remain untested. The scaling fits use seven Cerebras-GPT sizes and six Pythia sizes.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row cap is reached after keeping all per-size distractor logit shifts and the four-context scaling fits for each family. Left out the separately reported gold-token and overall (gold minus distractor) measures in Tables 3 and 5, relative-advantage fits in Table 1(b) and Tables 4 and 6, and additional visualizations in Figures 3–11.

untested.parts: No heads are identified and no previous-token-head composition or [A][B]…[A]→[B] pattern is measured. Random-token copying is a single-token repetition effect, not an induction-pattern test.
No training checkpoints, formation window, in-context-learning gain or loss bump.
No token-index loss and no attribution of in-context learning to induction heads in large models.
Two model families are studied, but induction heads are not located in either.
Training data and setup are not manipulated. Only the prompt's context type varies at inference.
No few-shot task learning and no comparison of head types or mechanisms.

record.verdict_notes: Row values were spot-checked against Tables 3–6 and are correct. All rows correctly carry versions ["none"]. The link to induction heads is interpretive and borrowed from Niu et al. (2025) and Olsson et al. (2022). No head-level evidence is given, so no verdict is possible on any version.

versions.untested_parts: No induction heads, previous-token-head composition, or [A][B] … [A] → [B] copying pattern are measured.
No training-time trajectory, abrupt formation window, in-context-learning gain by token position, or training-loss bump is measured.
The study does not measure induction heads or the share of large-model in-context learning carried by them; its logit-shift tests are not token-index loss measurements.
The study compares contextual entrainment across Cerebras-GPT and Pythia, but does not identify heads with induction behavior in those models or test other architectures or modalities.
Context types are varied, but the study does not manipulate training data or setup to test whether they determine induction-head formation or persistence of in-context learning.
No few-shot task learning or causal comparison of induction heads with other heads or mechanisms is tested.
No formation sequence or training-time transitions are measured.
